 GENERAL PUBLIC COMMENT
During each regular meeting, the Council shall provide a member of the public the opportunity to
address the City Council on any issue within the subject matter jurisdiction of the Council. Each
speaker shall be limited to three (3) minutes of general public comment at each regular meeting.
The City Council shall not discuss or take action relative to any general public comment unless
authorized by California Government Code Section 54954.Z(b).

AGENDA ORGANIZATION
This is the time for the Authority Board to discuss any changes in the order of agenda
items.

AGENDA ITEM PUBLIC COMMENT
The City Council shall provide an opportunity for the public to address the Council on
each agenda item before Council's consideration of the item. A member of the public
wishing to speak on one agenda item that is eligible for public comment shall be given
an opportunity to speak for up to three (3) minute when that item is considered by City
Council.

motion and one vote. There will be no separate discussion of these items. If discussion

separately.

The City Council, upon approval of the Consent Calendar will waive reading in full of all
ordinances and resolutions on the agenda and declare that said titles which appear on
the public agenda shall be determined to have been read by title and further reading
waived.

  DISTRICT ON A SEGMENT OF NORWALK BOULEVARD.

SUMMARY

The Community Development Director is requesting that the City Council approve
Resolution No. 092-2019 thereby considering the formation of the Underground Utility
District (UUD) No. 2019 -01 on a portion of Norwalk Boulevard; and

Set the Public hearing for the said UUD for October 8, 2019 and direct the City Clerk to
notify affected property owners as indicated in the resolution.

DISCUSSION

The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) Rule 20 sets policies and procedures
for the conversion of overhead power lines and other equipment to underground utilities,
a procedure called "undergrounding". Rule 20A projects are paid for by Southern
California Edison (SCE) ratepayers, not just those who live in locations where facilities
are to be underground.  Using CPUC formulas, SCE allocates rate funds to
communities for undergrounding based on previous allocations, the ratio of customers
served by overhead facilities to all the costumers in the community, and the fraction that
customers in the community represent to all SCE customers. City and County
Government choose these projects, using a process that includes public participation.
Because funds are limited and based on annual allocation, local governments often wait
and accumulate their allocations before starting and undergrounding project.

In the fall of 2018, staff met and had several conversations with SCE to coordinate,
locate and identify qualified potential projects to encumber allocated balance of Rule
20A funds for the City of Hawaiian Gardens, then valued at $881,822. The annual
allocation is $30,728. The yearly funding allocations are carried over into the fund
balance annually. The Southern California Edison and staff identified a segment of
 Norwalk Boulevard for formation of the undergrounding utility district to continue in the
beautification of the frontage of Norwalk Boulevard. The UUD limits were established
as Norwalk Boulevard from a point 100 feet south of southerly right-of-way line of
  th
Tilbury Street, proceeding north along Norwalk Boulevard to 100 feet north of 215
Street northerly right-of-way line and 100 feet west and east along Norwalk Boulevard
right-of- way limits. Due to estimated District construction cost of $1,100,000. The City
would be required to use the option to mortgage future Rule 20A funds up to next five
years.

The City's Municipal Code Chapter 13, establishes a procedure for the creation of
underground utility district and requires as the first step in such procedure the holding of
a public hearing to determine whether the public necessity, health, safety or welfare
requires the removal of overhead Utility infrastructure and the underground installation
of that infrastructure.

In order to move forward with the project and have SCE begin the undergrounding
effort, the City Council must adopt the required resolution, hold the public hearing, and
adopt an additional resolution to designate and establish the UUD.

FISCAL IMPACT

There is no fiscal impact for the consideration of the UUD.

RECOMMENDATION:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. 092-2019.
  2. Set the public hearing for said UUD for October 8, 2019 and direct the City Clerk
  to notify affected persons as indicated in the resolution.

SUBJECT:  DISCUSSION OF SPEED STUDY FOR NORWALK BOULEVARD FROM
  224TH STREET TO 226TH STREET, IN THE CITY OF HAWAIIAN
  GARDENS.

SUMMARY

At the August 27, 2019 Council meeting, Staff received direction to review the recently
completed Speed Survey of Norwalk Boulevard from 224th Street to 226 th Street and its
impacts to the Teen Center.

On January 22, 2018, Staff presented the completed Speed Survey of Norwalk
Boulevard from 224th Street to 226th Street. The speed study was completed following
the same standards of the recently approved City Wide Engineering and Traffic (E&T)
Survey.

The 2018 Speed Survey for Norwalk Boulevard was received and filed per Council
direction. Staff concurs with the findings and recommendations that no changes in the
speed limits for this section of Norwalk Boulevard are warranted.

In addition, this report will address questions raised by the Public Safety Commission as
part of the analysis.

BACKGROUND

The speed survey encompassed two (2) blocks of Norwalk Boulevard, from 224 th Street
to 226th Street, to address if there are any special circumstances that would warrant a
change in the speed limit.

The Vehicle Code requires that the survey be conducted based on the methodology
mandated by the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans). Caltrans directs
the methodology used for completing speed surveys to include an evaluation of current
vehicle speed, accident history, and conditions not readily apparent to the motorists.
This process is also required and is in compliance with the Manual of Uniform Traffic
Control Devices (MUTCD).
 The definition of an "Engineering and Traffic Survey" is contained in Section 627 of the
California Vehicle Code, (CVC).

The CVC has set certain regulations regarding the posting and enforcement of speed
zones. These regulations generally reflect the viewpoint that speed zoning should be
based on traffic conditions and natural driver behavior and not because of an arbitrary
response to a traffic event, occurrences or future concerns. This concept is known as
the "basic speed law."

All fifty states of the United States base their speed regulations on the Basic Speed
Law. In California, eve 22350 defines the basic speed law.

This law recognizes that driving conditions vary widely from time-to-time and place-to-
place; therefore, no set or fixed driving rules will adequately serve all conditions. The
motorists will constantly adjust their driving behavior to fit the conditions they encounter.
Driver must learn to do this with a minimum assistance from law enforcement. The
Basic Speed Law is founded on the belief that most motorists can modify their driving
behavior properly, if they are aware of the conditions around them.

State law, CVC 22357 authorizes local authorities to lower the maximum speed limit (65
mph) or to raise the speed limit in business and residential districts (25 mph) based on a
traffic and engineering survey. These intermediate speed limits between 25 and 65 mph
must be posted to clearly define the limits of the zone and the prima facie speed.

The MUTCD, California Edition, Section 28.116 Speed Limits and Zones specifies a
method of providing an Engineering and Traffic Survey of speed limits on City and
County roadways and local streets.

DISCUSSION

The current posted speed limit on Norwalk Boulevard from the south City limits to
Carson Street is 40 miles per hour. This speed limit was justified in the recently adopted
Citywide Engineering and Traffic Survey.

The findings and recommendations of the Norwalk Boulevard between 224th Street and
226 th Street speed survey do not warrant the speed limit on Norwalk Boulevard be
changed for this street segment. This report confirms the speed limits from the Citywide
Engineering and Traffic Survey.

Staff has initiated a request for additional accident data from January 2018 to August
2019. Staff contacted the Highway Patrol to obtain the accident data. Staff will present
the data upon request. Staff is only aware of one (1) accident; the driving under the
influence (DUI) driver that hit the landscape wall of the Teen Center prior to completion
of the Teen Center during this time frame.

As part of the analysis, the Public Safety Commission asked several questions and
responses are provided.

  1. How many times has the speed limit changed from the year 2000 to now?
 Staff reviewed the Engineering and Traffic Surveys from 2000 and found the City
completed surveys in 2002, 2013 and the recently approved 2018 surveys to set speed
limits Citywide. The speed limit changed only once, in 2002.

  2. When was the most recent change?

The speed limit was increased, based on the 2002 Survey from 35 miles per hour (mph)
to 40 mph. The Traffic Engineer, in 2002 recommended the increase in the speed limit.

  3. How has the speed limit changed?

The speed limit was increased based on the recommendations from the 2002 Survey,
from 35 mph to 40 mph.

  4. What is the speed limit now?

The 2018 Engineering and Traffic Survey and the Speed Survey of Norwalk Boulevard
from 224 th Street to 226th Street confirmed the speed limit of 40 mph.

  5. How can it be lowered?

Per the CVC and MUTCD, speed limits are established based on the Engineering and
Traffic Survey for the conditions at the time of the survey. The CVC allows the Traffic
Engineer to lower the speed limit 5 mph based on site conditions and other mitigating
factors. Typical commercial or 'Teen Center" operations do not qualify as "other"
mitigating factors.

As your City Engineer, the eve and MUTCD clearly state the process and method of
determining the speed limits on the City streets. I cannot recommend a speed limit
change that is in conflict with the data of the survey.

The City Council controls the streets and can make decisions regarding the
establishment of speed limits on City streets. If speed limits are changed from the
Engineering and Traffic Survey recommendations, law enforcement will not be able to
use "radar" for speed enforcement but would have to employ other methods for speed
enforcement.

If the speed limits are changed from the Engineering and Traffic Survey
recommendations, the liability exposure protections afforded to the City by the Survey,
eve and MUTCD would be negated. Thereby, unduly exposing the City to liability and
exposure if accidents occur in that area if the Council directed changes to speed limit
postings.

FISCAL IMPACT

The is no fiscal impact with regards to this report.

RECOMMENDATION

The City Engineer recommends no changes in the posted speed limits on Norwalk
Boulevard from 224th Street to 226th Street.
